Dear all,

 

Please see the attached letter received this afternoon from JLG. This letter states on an open basis that
“JLG does not have any agreement with any Case Lead to begin employment with JLG prior to the end of their notice period with your client and does not intend to enter into any such agreement”
which, if true, is helpful.

 

Simultaneously we have received the below response from Jones Chase (acting for Gallagher):-

 

“Dear Clyde & Co

 

By way of courtesy, please note that our client does not intend to provide a substantive response to your letter of 17 October 2025.

 

Our client is not involved in the matters raised therein which are considered an internal matter for Pogust Goodhead. Our client otherwise adopts the same position as set out in the response sent by JLG earlier
 today.

 

Yours faithfully

 

Jones Chase Employment Lawyers”

 

Clearly, neither JLG nor Gallagher have answered our questions.

 

The question, therefore, is to what extent we go back to them and/or convey to Burke that JLG have told us that they aren’t starting there before 15 December 2025. I appreciate that this is more of a commercial question than a
 legal one. Subject to your thoughts, my sense is to leave it just now with JLG and Gallagher and monitor where we get to with Burke/ the alleged protected disclosure before replying further.

 

Grateful for your thoughts.

 

Best wishes,

 

Charlie

Dear James and Jonathan,

I hope you're well.


I am writing regarding the Pan-NOx Emissions Litigation, specifically regarding the viability of securing additional LOI coverage through further excess layer insurance
 policies.


Following the handing down of the judgment (10th September 2025) after the Second Costs Management Hearing (15-16 July 2025), the Defendants have revisited their
 position on applications for security for costs. We have therefore undertaken a further review of the potential adverse costs resulting from the Tranche 3 Quantum Trial and the Second General Budget. 


Previously, our assessment of ATE sufficiency was calculated on the following basis:



60% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



60% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to Spring 2026.


Given the level of incurred costs and the criticisms between Defendants regarding their figures, we consider that the sufficiency calculation can be revised downwards
 without materially affecting the adequacy of coverage. We propose the following revised basis:



50% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



50% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to 31 July 2026.


On this revised basis, the following GLOs fall below the proposed coverage threshold:


 




Mercedes 



-£953,580.35





Ford



-£838,961.27





Renault-Nissan



-£2,535,219.93





PCD



-£149,635.79





Toyota



-£136,927.40






 


We would be grateful for your confirmation on whether additional excess layer coverage can be secured for these cases, specifically for Mercedes, Ford, and Renault-Nissan.


We look forward to hearing from you as soon as possible.


Kind regards,

My email confirms the outcome of the grievance process. 1. Summary of Your Grievance  Your grievance raised the following main issues:Stress and adverse health effects, which you attribute to actions or omissions of senior leadership following the case leads’ resignationsPerceived lack of acknowledgement or response to you and colleagues regarding various concerns raised in emailsConduct during the case-leads meeting on 24 October 2025, specifically a comment made by Anna Varga, Lead Emissions partner,  about the potential move of staff to JLGBroader concerns about senior leadership, culture, media activity, and the leak of the interim report, which you indicated contributed to embarrassment, stress and concerns about the firm’s governanceA request for remedies to include an acknowledgement of stress caused by the firm, an apology and compensationA request to leave immediately after the conclusion of the PCD phase of the trial (28 November 2025), rather than complete your contractual notice period ending 15 December 2025.2. Findings2.1 Responses to concerns raised by case leadsYou expressed frustration that your emails and those of colleagues did not receive the responses you expected. Having reviewed the relevant correspondence, I acknowledge that some responses were delayed or brief. Responses were provided on a number of occasions, although they did not always address every point raised in depth. It is clear that senior leadership have been operating under significant time pressure during an exceptionally active phase of litigation, which affected the level of detail they were able to provide. Having reviewed the correspondence, I have found no evidence that any delays or brevity in replies were intended to ignore or dismiss your concerns.2.2 Stress and adverse health effectsYou described experiencing stress and having sought advice from a mental health nurse, who recommended self-certification. You explained that you continued working due to your commitment to the trial and clients.The firm does take well-being seriously and your comment on the impact on you is noted. I have found no evidence that the firm engaged in conduct intended to cause you stress. The pressures you described appear to arise primarily from the ongoing challenges we face with our litigation and the organisational changes underway. While I recognise that you personally experienced stress, I have not found evidence of unreasonable treatment or any breach of duty by the firm. Whilst you confirmed in our meeting that you did not require any personal adjustments, you remain encouraged to use all available wellbeing resources, including visiting your doctor as advised by the medical nurse, as well as the employee assistance programme and your private medical insurance. If you wish to discuss any additional support we can offer you, I remain available to assist you.2.3 The 24 October meetingYou raised concerns regarding a comment made by Anna Varga, which you felt was factually wrong and unhelpful. In reviewing this matter,  my view is that the comment was made without the intention you inferred; however, I do fully accept that it did not reflect the facts, as it is correct that not all staff leaving the firm are moving to JLG and you are right to point this out. 2.4 Concerns regarding senior leadership, public communications, governance matters and disclosure of the interim reportYou raised several concerns relating to the wider conduct of senior leadership, including:Embarrassment caused by public statements or media exchanges involving the firm Alleged tensions or disputes between senior individualsThe governance structure of the firm and its alignment with litigation strategyThe leak of an interim report to the media.I fully acknowledge that these issues have caused you concern and that you perceive them as contributing to the pressures you have experienced and I also recognise that they may have affected the broader working environment for both you and your colleagues. However, after careful consideration, I must confirm that these matters relate to organisational governance, strategic communications and the conduct of senior individuals in their executive capacities and therefore do not relate specifically to your individual employment relationship or fall within the scope of the grievance procedure. In addition, several of the concerns you raised, particularly regarding the interim report leak and media activity, are already being considered through separate internal processes and cannot be managed through the grievance route. While I recognise that you understandably have strong views about these issues and feel they contributed to the stress you experienced, the evidence available does not indicate that they resulted in targeted or unreasonable treatment towards you as an individual.3. RemedyYou requested an acknowledgement that the firm caused you stress, an apology, and compensation. After considering all of the information available, I do not find that the firm’s actions constituted unreasonable treatment, misconduct, or a breach of duty. Accordingly, I cannot conclude that the firm was responsible for causing the stress you describe and an apology would therefore not be appropriate in circumstances where the grievance has not been upheld. For the same reason, compensation is not warranted. That said, I recognise the pressures you have been under and am sorry that you have experienced this period as distressing. Although this does not amount to an acceptance of fault, I do want to acknowledge the impact you described during our meeting.4. Request to Leave After the PCD PhaseDuring our meeting, you indicated a wish to conclude your employment after the PCD phase of the PDD Trial ends on 28 November 2025, rather than work until the end of your contractual notice period on 15 December 2025. I have discussed the matter with Anna Varga and unfortunately, we are unable to accommodate your request to leave earlier. A full and thorough handover is essential to ensure continuity and to meet our client obligations. Your continued availability is also necessary to support colleagues who will be assuming your responsibilities. For these reasons, you are required to work your full notice period, ending on 15 December 2025, in accordance with your employment contract. We will, of course, work with you to ensure that the handover process is structured, manageable and appropriately supported.5. Support Going ForwardI appreciate the candid and constructive manner in which you raised your concerns. I will continue to support you throughout the remainder of your notice period. Should you wish to discuss workload management, handover planning, or wellbeing resources, please let me know.6. Right of AppealYou are entitled to submit a written appeal within 10 working days of receiving this letter to @HR Team, setting out the grounds of your appeal.  Thank Dear all,



I hope you are all well. I write further to my last update on 5 August 2025, to provide you with a brief update on the following matters as they relate to the Ford NOx Emissions
 Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally (the “Litigation”):


·        
PDD Trial Preparation;

·        
Claimants Mechanical Expert;

·        
Quantum Trial and discontinuance;

·        
Change in personnel.


PDD Trial Preparation and final Pre-Trial Review



We are fast approaching the commencement of the PDD Trial, with the first day of trial listed for 13 October 2025, and the trial due to run until 19 December 2025.



Our skeleton argument was filed and served on 19 September, representing a mammoth undertaking by the entire Solicitor team and the barristers. The Ford specific annex to
 the skeleton argument was filed and served on 24 September. There was a slight extension to the Ford annex on account of the Defendants providing a very late second witness statement from a Ford employee. While we were not obliged to permit this into evidence,
 we took the view after considering it, that the statement was in fact more helpful for us and the case to allow its entry, rather than refusing permissions. As a caveat to our permittance of its inclusion, we agreed a short extension to the Ford annex.



As soon as I am in a position to provide you with a copy of the skeleton argument (with redactions for confidential information) I will send this to you. I would hope this

De-designation Hearing
(“DDH”)



One key hurdle the parties face in these Pan-NOx Litigations is that there are significant barriers erected between the Litigations that prevent the efficient and effective
 exchange and comparison of information and disclosure between the cases. This is a fundamental part of the Claimants claim i.e. that many of the manufacturers were either sharing strategies and technology to insert prohibits defeat devices (“PDDs”)
 in their vehicles, or alternatively, that better technology was available that was being used by other manufacturers that mean the Defendants did not need to insert PDDs in their vehicles.



As mentioned in previous updates, much the information that exists in the Ford Litigation, and similarly in the other Lead Cases (Mercedes, Renault/Nissan and Peugeot Citroën)
 is subject to a case specific Confidentiality Ring Orders (“CRO”). Each of the Lead cases has their own CRO. The Defendants have taken this CRO as a means to try and keep secret the majority of the documentation that they have provided to us, thereby
 restricting access to the documents to persons who are members of the CRO. Despite protestations from the Defendants, we have successfully implemented a Pan-Lead CRO, which has been constructed to assist in the sharing of confidential information across the
 cases. While this is helpful in permitted us to see documents from other cases, it does not alleviate the issue of transferring documents into the Pan-Lead CRO (as the Defendants continue to raise various issues regarding this) and it does not prevent those
 documents being confidential and only certain people being able to see them. This does not go to the principle of open justice, whereby the public should know the conduct of these manufacturers. It is and always has been our intention to seek to de-designate
 these documents so that they can be referred to openly and in public.



The DDH is shaped at doing precisely that; bringing those documents into the public and also to make the process of hearing these cases in court more feasible. Under present
 circumstances, any time a party wishes to discuss any documentation that is confidential, it would require the Court room to be emptied of people who are not within the CROs, which is simply unworkable. The DDH is intended to allow open justice to be carried
 out. 



The Claimants prepared and filed their respective applications and witness evidence on 13 June 2025 and we took receipt of the Defendants’ responsive evidence late last night.

Alicia, this is our recommendation beneath. In short:

 

a.     
We can’t totally ignore the case leads

b.     
Tell LD (and counsel) the AA can’t be finalised before the PTR

c.     
Speak to LD after the PTR to make necessary changes

d.     
Then speak to case leads to tell them about changes, and for the rest they need to get with the picture

 


The emails back and forth with this team is getting us nowhere. We think there needs to be a meeting with them, attended by Alicia and Anna. That obviously can’t be before the PTR, so would need to
 be on Tuesday at the earliest. But it might even have to be Wednesday. We would prepare you for this.
Their overwhelming issue is the delegation of work by LD to individual solicitors at PG. This has always seemed problematic to us, but LD would not budge. We presumed that in practice, things would
 continue to work as they have done up to now, and Martyn Day seemed to confirm that – but the language remains different.



To be clear, we are not conceding the principle that the case leads have the right to consent to this agreement – but they can’t just be ignored.



We consider (but should get it cleared by Clydes) that there is nothing inherently wrong or out of the ordinary with an employer telling an employee to do, for a limited period and for specific work,
 what a responsible third party tells it to do – as long as the employer continues to oversee and supervise (including in the SRA sense) the employee. So if the employer considers the employee is nor being directed properly, it can tell the employee not longer
 to follow the directions of the third party.
But that situation is not precisely what we have, because of the word “solely” in the Agency Agreement, where it relates to LD’s supervision of PG personnel doing the Common Work delegated
 to them. That makes it appear that only LD will know what the PG employees will do, so PG can no longer supervise them.
So what is the way forward? We suggest the following:



Tell LD (and counsel) now that we will not be able to agree the AA before the PTR, and that we will need to speak to them after the PTR. During that discussion, give them a summary of the case leads’
 concerns, remind them that they want and need to work with the case leads, and the only way we can see this getting anywhere is if we drop the word “solely”. We must also tell them that (subject to Clydes agreeing this is acceptable) PG will let the
 employees know it is authorising them to do the work at LD’s direction on a limited basis (Common Work only), that PG will retain oversight and supervision, and if PG considers that any direction is improper (eg, a breach of regulations), it will have the
 right to rescind our instructions to the employees to follow LD’s directions. We see this as the only way forward. Since Natasha has already been in contact with Martyn, it may be that she needs to deliver this message.
At the same time, have Clydes look at the case leads’ letter and the agency agreement (with and without the word “solely”) and get their view on the employment law aspects (and how far we can push
 things). Clydes should also confirm that they see no employment issues with the way we are proposing to resolve this (which should not be an issue). Raminder can draft an employment response, but it should
not be sent until we have reviewed it and determined if it should be sent, consistent with our strategy.



When you meet the case leads on Tuesday (?), therefore, you will hopefully be able to say PG has amended the agreement, it is clear PG remains their supervisors, and you can be super-robust about
 everything else.



We would also suggest that after that meeting, you have a follow-up with them and Martyn Day, but we have to make sure Martyn is on side before suggesting that.



As for the PTR, there is
no way we can agree the agency agreement (and any side letter) before then, so we will need to tell the court we’re in the final stages of agreeing it.
Ben Williams KC should be told that the agency agreement is being finalised –if necessary, he can say that is being done in consultation with the case leads. He can say that the case leads will be
 working their notice, which ends 15/19 Dec, but shouldn’t say anything more positive than that.

Dear Anna, 



Thank you for your email. 



We have some overarching points to raise before addressing the points in your email regarding the Side Letter Agency Agreement (“SL AA”). 



First and foremost, we have raised serious and significant issues regarding how traumatic we, and the entire team, are finding this process and that we have genuine
 concerns for the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those
 concerns, nor does it even mention them. 



We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work
 and non-PDD Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything
 we have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on
 critical workstreams.  



Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions
 and, in aid of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness
 statements. You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board,
 despite Pogust Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that
 dismisses our concerns and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  



For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this
 has been put in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement
 either does not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted
 and the intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  



If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious
 engagement from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  



We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. 



On the points in your email: 


1.                  
Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter 


You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged”
within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding
 that the new arrangement is entirely novel.  



 



You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear
 that it goes further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects: 



 



a.
Formal separation of supervision and control 



The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG.
 Indeed, we understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx
 AA. That agreement permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the
supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations. 



 



b.
Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions 



The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy
 or reassign its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer. 



 



The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that
 “this will not practically change much day to day.”  



 


2.                  
Tension with Employment Contracts 


Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there
 will be no change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. 



Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly
 conflicts with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract: 


 

a.
Duty of obedience and supervision 

Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to
 comply with PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD
 in respect of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract. 

 

b.
Regulatory oversight 

The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the
 supervising solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?  

 

These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.  

 

c. Consent and legal clarity 

The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains
 the employer, yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise. 


 


3.                  
Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk 
The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing
 common work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is
 responsible for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here. 


 



This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval
 from PG's insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly,
whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA. 



 



This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability.
 The SL AA unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure. 



 



We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue. 



 


4.                  
Client Consent 


If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the
 informed consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the
 direction of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make
 informed decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can. 
 
You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by
 the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these
 circumstances. 



Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  


·               
You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations
 that PG has made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us
 have informed you of our plans post-PG.  

 

·               
You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from
 counsel – as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting
 this afternoon.” In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution. 

 

·               
You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to
 non-common work? 


We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial
 beginning in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism.
 It alters the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external
 law firm (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of
 ensuring compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. 



We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those
 issues and how they can be addressed, such that we can move forward, together.   The Case Leads

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure
 you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that
 I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such,
 I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into
 the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim
 back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the
 employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm
 has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts
 on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into
 hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover
 the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.
